title: What to Pack for Disney: The Honest Park Bag
h1: What to Pack for a Disney Park Day
metaDescription: An honest park bag list for Walt Disney World and Disneyland, including the popular items that do nothing in Florida humidity and the ones worth every gram.
summary: Category-by-category packing for a Disney park day, with Orlando humidity and Anaheim dry heat treated as the different problems they are, and a candid list of what to leave at home.
intro: You will walk between eight and twelve miles on a full Disney park day and carry everything you pack for all of it. That single fact should govern the entire list. Every item has to earn its weight, and the most common packing mistake is not forgetting something — it is bringing a bag so heavy that your shoulders hurt by lunchtime and you leave it in a locker.

The second thing to get right is climate, because Orlando and Anaheim present opposite problems. Florida is hot and humid, which means sweat does not evaporate and evaporative cooling gadgets barely work. Southern California is hot and dry, with cold mornings and genuinely cold evenings, which means layers matter and misting fans actually do something. A packing list that treats the two the same is a packing list written by someone who has only been to one of them.

This page carries affiliate links, so here is the deal plainly: nothing appears on this list that we would not carry ourselves, several popular products are named specifically so you can avoid buying them, and where the honest answer is that you do not need to buy anything, that is what it says. A list that recommends everything is worth nothing to you and we would rather have the trust.
keyPoints: Weight is the constraint. You carry every item for ten miles, and the bag you regret is always the heavy one.
Orlando is humid: evaporative cooling gadgets — misting fans, cooling towels, neck fans — do very little there.
Anaheim is dry with cold mornings and evenings: a layer you can tie around your waist matters more than any cooling device.
Moisture-wicking socks and blister tape applied before you feel anything are the two highest-value items on the whole list.
One 10,000 mAh battery per two people, with a short cable each. Phone dead means no tickets, no Lightning Lane, and no mobile order.
Tag your stroller. They are moved by Cast Members into parking rows and they all look identical.
Balloons are not permitted at Animal Kingdom, stroller wagons are not permitted at either resort, and loose ice is not allowed in coolers.

sections.heading: Orlando humidity versus Anaheim dry heat
body: These are different problems and they need different kit. Central Florida runs hot with very high humidity for a large part of the year, plus reliable afternoon thunderstorms through the warm months. Sweat does not evaporate efficiently in that air, which is why you stay wet, why you overheat faster than the temperature suggests, and why a misting fan achieves almost nothing — the air is already saturated.

Southern California is the opposite. Daytime heat is dry, which means shade and airflow work, evaporative cooling genuinely helps, and you dehydrate without noticing because you are not visibly sweating. Mornings and evenings drop sharply even in summer, and a marine layer can keep the first half of a summer morning grey and cool. Anyone who has packed only shorts for Anaheim in June has stood in a queue at 9 PM regretting it.

Rain is the other divergence. Florida rain is a heavy, brief, near-daily afternoon event in the warm months — a poncho and twenty minutes indoors handles it. Anaheim rain is rare, and when it does arrive it is persistent drizzle rather than a downpour, which a hood handles better than a poncho does.

callout.title: The neck fan question, answered honestly
callout.body: Battery-powered neck fans and misting devices are the most heavily marketed park accessory and they are close to useless in Orlando. Moving saturated air across skin that cannot evaporate sweat does very little, and you have carried a battery-powered object all day for it. In Anaheim's dry heat the same device works well. Buy one for California; skip it for Florida.

sections.heading: Feet: the category that decides your trip
body: More Disney days are ruined by feet than by weather, queues, or children. Ten miles a day on hard surfaces, in heat, for four or five consecutive days is a physical demand most people do not otherwise place on themselves, and the failure mode — blisters — is entirely preventable and entirely miserable once it happens.

Wear shoes you have already walked twenty miles in. A new pair bought for the trip is the single most reliable way to lose a park day. Support matters more than cushioning; a stiff-soled shoe you can walk in all day beats a soft one that lets your foot spread and rub. Sandals are for the pool, not the park, and flip-flops on a rope drop morning are an act of self-harm.

Socks are underrated to an almost comic degree. Cotton socks hold sweat against your skin and are the direct cause of most blisters. Synthetic or wool-blend running socks wick moisture away and cost very little, and they are the highest-return item on this entire page. Bring one clean pair per day plus a spare in the bag.

Tape before you feel anything. Blister tape or a lubricating balm applied to your heels and toes at the hotel, in the morning, prevents the friction that causes damage. Applying it after you feel a hot spot is damage control; applying it before is prevention. Experienced visitors do this every single morning without thinking about it.

items: Shoes with at least twenty miles already on them. Never a new pair.
Synthetic or wool-blend socks, one pair per day plus a spare in the bag. No cotton.
Blister tape or an anti-friction balm, applied in the morning before you feel anything.
A second pair of shoes for Florida, so a soaked pair can dry overnight.
Compression socks for the flight and, for a lot of people, for the park day itself.
Plasters and a blister kit in the bag, because prevention sometimes fails and every park's First Aid has them but you will be twenty minutes away.

sections.heading: Weather, sun, and rain
body: Sunscreen is the item people bring and then do not use. A high-SPF lotion applied at the hotel and reapplied at lunch is the standard, and the reapplication is the part that gets skipped. A stick format for faces makes reapplying a five-second act rather than a production, which is the only reason it actually happens.

Hats with a full brim beat caps, and both beat nothing. In Florida the light is diffuse and you burn without feeling hot; in California it is direct and relentless. Sunglasses are a genuine comfort item rather than a style one, particularly for anyone sensitive to glare or prone to headaches.

For Florida rain, a cheap poncho bought before you travel is the right answer. The in-park versions cost several times more for the same plastic, and the storms are heavy enough that an umbrella is awkward in a crowd and useless in wind. Ponchos also keep a stroller and its contents dry, which an umbrella cannot.

For Anaheim, pack a light layer with a hood instead. It handles the rare drizzle, it handles a 60-degree evening in the queue for Radiator Springs Racers, and it ties around your waist for the eight hours you do not need it.

items: High-SPF sunscreen, plus a stick format for faces so reapplying actually happens.
A brimmed hat. Caps leave your ears and neck exposed and both burn.
Sunglasses — a comfort item, not a fashion one, particularly for glare-sensitive eyes.
Ponchos bought before you travel, for Florida. One per person, packed flat.
A light hooded layer for Anaheim, year round, no exceptions.
Lip balm with sun protection. The most forgotten item on any list and the one you notice by day two.
A microfibre towel the size of a paperback, for water rides and for drying a bench after rain.

callout.title: The wet ride problem
callout.body: Grizzly River Run at California Adventure and Kali River Rapids at Animal Kingdom soak you properly, and both are outdoors in a place where you then walk around for six hours. A gallon zip bag for phones and wallets costs nothing, and a pair of quick-drying socks in the bag turns a squelching afternoon into a two-minute inconvenience. Do the ride, then change your socks on the nearest bench.

sections.heading: Tech
body: Your phone is your ticket, your Lightning Lane, your mobile order, your map, your camera, and the way you find your family. A dead phone is not an inconvenience at a Disney park; it is the end of your ability to do most things. Battery management is therefore the single most important tech decision you make.

One 10,000 mAh power bank per two people, with a short cable for each person, covers a full day comfortably. Bring short cables rather than long ones — a six-inch cable lets you charge in a pocket while you walk, a three-foot cable becomes a trip hazard in a queue. Both resorts sell and rent swap-style batteries at kiosks, which are convenient and modest in capacity; if you already own a decent power bank, bring it instead.

Turn brightness down, turn background app refresh off, and put the phone in low-power mode before you leave the hotel rather than at 4 PM when it is already at fifteen per cent. The Disney app is a heavy application that uses location services constantly, and it will drain a phone faster than anything else you run.

Everything else is optional. A phone case with a lanyard loop is genuinely useful on rides where you are holding on. Selfie sticks are prohibited at both resorts. A separate camera is a lovely thing to have and a heavy thing to carry, and most people who bring one on day one leave it in the room by day three.

items: One 10,000 mAh power bank per two people. More capacity than that is more weight than you need.
Short charging cables, six inches or so, one per person. Long cables tangle and trip people.
A phone case with a lanyard or wrist strap. Rides with restraints are where phones get dropped.
Gallon zip bags for water rides. Cheap, weightless, and they also work as a sick bag.
Low-power mode enabled before you leave the hotel, not after the battery warning.
Skip the selfie stick — prohibited at both resorts — and think hard about a separate camera.

sections.heading: Kids
body: The kids category is where packing lists inflate the most, and where the honest answer is that four or five items carry almost all the value.

A full change of clothes for anyone under about six is non-negotiable — water rides, spilled drinks, and accidents all happen, and a wet child in air conditioning is a miserable child. Pack it in a zip bag so the wet clothes have somewhere to go afterwards.

Snacks matter more than any toy. The pre-meltdown window in a small child is short and a bag of something familiar buys you fifteen minutes to reach a restaurant. Keep it in an outside pocket, not buried, because you will need it in a queue with no room to open a bag properly.

And tag your stroller. Cast Members move parked strollers into tidy rows constantly, and every third stroller at a Disney park is the same model in the same colour. A bright ribbon on the handle, a luggage tag with your phone number, or a strip of patterned tape turns a fifteen-minute hunt into a five-second one. This is the tip that experienced parents give and packing lists never mention.

items: A full change of clothes per child under six, in a zip bag that then holds the wet ones.
Familiar snacks in an outside pocket, reachable inside a queue.
A stroller tag — ribbon, luggage tag, or patterned tape. Cast Members will move your stroller and they all look alike.
A stroller rain cover for Florida, which doubles as a way to keep the seat dry while you are on a ride.
Child-sized over-ear defenders for anyone sound-sensitive. Permitted on every attraction and better than any other intervention.
One comfort item, and one only. More than one and you will lose something that matters.
Sun hats that fasten. Unfastened hats last approximately one ride.

callout.title: Wagons are not permitted
callout.body: Stroller wagons are prohibited at both resorts, and strollers themselves are limited to roughly 31 inches wide by 52 inches long. If you are renting from a third party, confirm the model complies before it is delivered — being turned away at security with a wagon and two tired toddlers is a bad way to start a day.

sections.heading: Medical
body: A small pouch of medical basics saves you a twenty-minute walk to First Aid at the exact moment you least want to take one. Keep it small and keep it in the same pocket every day so anybody in the party can find it.

Prescriptions travel in their original labelled containers, with more days' supply than the trip requires in case of travel delays. If anything needs refrigeration, First Aid stations at every park will store it — that service exists and almost nobody knows about it.

The over-the-counter list is short and specific: pain relief, an antihistamine, an anti-diarrhoeal, motion sickness tablets if anyone is prone, blister plasters, and electrolyte tablets or sachets. That last one is the item that most improves a hot day and that almost nobody packs. Water alone does not replace what you lose sweating for ten hours, and the difference between plain water and water with electrolytes on a August afternoon in Florida is genuinely noticeable.

Every park has a First Aid station with air conditioning, beds, and registered nurses. It is free, it is not only for emergencies, and using it for a lie-down when someone is overheating is exactly what it is for.

items: Prescriptions in original labelled containers, with spare days built in.
Electrolyte tablets or sachets. The most under-packed item on any Disney list.
Pain relief, an antihistamine, an anti-diarrhoeal, and motion sickness tablets if anyone is prone.
Blister plasters and a small roll of tape.
Hand sanitiser and a few antiseptic wipes.
Anti-chafe balm for anyone walking ten miles in heat. Unglamorous and it will save your trip.

sections.heading: Food and water
body: Both resorts allow outside food and non-alcoholic drinks, within a bag size limit and with the exceptions of glass containers, alcohol, and loose ice. Reusable ice packs are fine. This is the largest single saving available to a family and it takes ten minutes of preparation the night before.

A refillable water bottle is essential, and every quick-service counter at both resorts will give you a cup of ice water free if you ask. There is no purchase requirement and no catch. A collapsible bottle takes up nothing in a bag when empty, which is the difference between carrying one and leaving it in the room.

Carry the food that survives a bag at 90 degrees: nuts, dried fruit, crackers, protein bars, pretzels. Anything with chocolate will not survive Florida, and anything that needs refrigeration should not be attempted. Fruit that bruises is a false economy.

The hybrid approach most experienced families settle on is carrying breakfast and snacks and buying one proper meal in the park. It saves real money, removes the 8 AM hotel food court queue, and means you never have to make a decision about food while somebody is already too hungry to make one.

callout.title: Free ice water at every counter
callout.body: Ask any quick-service counter at either resort for a cup of ice water and you will get one at no charge. No purchase, no argument. For a family of four doing this three or four times a day across a week, that is a meaningful sum, and it removes the single most indefensible purchase in the park.

sections.heading: The bag itself, and what is not allowed in
body: A small backpack or a crossbody bag, worn on the front in crowds. Both resorts screen bags at entry and the no-bag lane is significantly faster, so on a rope drop morning, consolidating everything into one adult's pockets is worth fifteen minutes. Bag size limits apply at both resorts — roughly 24 inches long by 15 inches wide by 18 inches high — and coolers are permitted within that.

Lockers are available near the entrances at every park and are worth the money on a day when you have brought a change of clothes for a water ride or bought something you do not want to carry. Do not carry a shopping bag around a park all afternoon; both resorts will hold purchases for collection, and Walt Disney World resort guests can have in-park purchases delivered to their hotel.

The prohibited list is short and worth knowing before you queue for security. Selfie sticks, glass containers other than small baby food jars, loose ice, alcohol, weapons of any kind, drones, wagons, and marijuana or CBD products in any form are all refused at both resorts. Animal Kingdom additionally prohibits balloons and plastic straws and lids, for animal safety — buy the balloon at Magic Kingdom instead.

sections.heading: What to leave at home
body: This is the section the packing lists skip, and it is the one that makes the biggest difference to how your shoulders feel at 6 PM. Every item below is widely recommended and most people do not use it.

Neck fans and misting devices in Florida, as covered above — physics is not on your side in that humidity. Cooling towels have the same problem. Full-size umbrellas, which are unwieldy in a crowd and useless in a Florida downpour. Autograph books, which sound charming and which a meaningful proportion of children lose interest in by the second day; a photograph with the character achieves the same thing and weighs nothing.

Also: more than one comfort toy, a separate camera you have not used in a year, a full picnic set, laminated itineraries, glow sticks bought in bulk, and any clothing item you would be upset to have soaked. Both resorts will provide the day's genuine surprises; you do not need to carry contingency for all of them.

The honest summary of this whole page: shoes, socks, water, sunscreen, a battery, and snacks. Everything else on this list is an optimisation. If you get those six right, you will have a good day with a light bag, and if you get them wrong, nothing else you packed will rescue it.

items: Neck fans, misting fans, and cooling towels — for Florida. They work fine in Anaheim.
Full-size umbrellas. A poncho does the job in a fraction of the space.
Autograph books, unless your child has specifically asked for one and will carry it themselves.
A separate camera, unless photography is genuinely why you are going.
Laminated itineraries and printed plans. Your phone has them and plans change by 10 AM.
More than one comfort item per child.
Anything you would be upset to lose. Things get dropped from ride vehicles and not all of them come back.

callout.title: About the links on this page
callout.body: This page carries affiliate links, which means we may earn a commission if you buy through them at no additional cost to you. That is precisely why several widely-marketed park products are named above as things not to buy. If the honest answer is that you already own something good enough, or that the item does not work in the climate you are visiting, that is what this page says.

faqs.q: What is the single most important thing to pack?
faqs.a: Shoes you have already broken in, worn with synthetic or wool-blend socks rather than cotton. Feet ruin more Disney days than weather or crowds, the damage is cumulative across a multi-day trip, and it is almost entirely preventable. Tape your heels in the morning before you feel anything.

faqs.q: Do neck fans and cooling towels work at Disney?
faqs.a: In Anaheim's dry heat, yes — evaporative cooling works well there. In Orlando's humidity they do very little, because the air is already close to saturated and sweat cannot evaporate. They are among the most heavily marketed park accessories and among the least useful things you can carry in Florida.

faqs.q: Can I bring food and drink into the parks?
faqs.a: Yes, at both resorts, within a bag size limit. Glass containers other than small baby food jars, alcohol, and loose ice are not permitted; reusable ice packs are fine. Carrying breakfast and snacks is the single largest saving available to a family, and every counter will give you free ice water.

faqs.q: How big a power bank do I need?
faqs.a: One 10,000 mAh bank per two people covers a full day with room to spare. Bring short cables rather than long ones so you can charge in a pocket while walking. Put your phone in low-power mode before you leave the hotel, because the Disney app uses location services constantly and drains a battery faster than anything else you run.

faqs.q: What is banned at Disney park security?
faqs.a: Selfie sticks, glass containers other than baby food jars, loose ice, alcohol brought from outside, weapons, drones, and wagons including stroller wagons. Marijuana and CBD products are prohibited in any form even where legal locally. Animal Kingdom additionally bans balloons and plastic straws and lids for animal safety.

faqs.q: Do I need a stroller if my child is four or five?
faqs.a: Often yes, even for children who do not use one at home. Eight to twelve miles a day is a very different demand from a normal week, and a stroller doubles as somewhere to store the bag. Tag it clearly — Cast Members move parked strollers into rows and every third one is the same model in the same colour.

faqs.q: Should I pack differently for Disneyland than for Walt Disney World?
faqs.a: Yes, and mainly in two ways. Anaheim needs a layer with a hood for cold mornings and evenings, year round. Orlando needs ponchos for near-daily afternoon storms in the warm months, a second pair of shoes so a soaked pair can dry, and none of the evaporative cooling gear that works in California.
